readings.c1s1:
¶
'''booming'''<sup>2</sup> (bö′ming), ''p. a.'' [Ppr. of ''boom''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] Active; lively; advancing; buoyant: as, a ''booming'' market. [U. S.]

'''boom-iron''' (böm′ī″ėrn), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a metal ring on a yard, through which a studdingsail-boom is run in and out.
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Boom-iron on yard-arm.}}}}

'''boom-jigger''' (böm′jig″ėr), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', the small purchase used in rigging out a studdingsail-boom, and, by shifting the tackle, in rigging it in. Also called ''in-and-out jigger''.

'''boomkin''' (böm′kin), ''n.'' Same as ''bumkin''.

'''boom-mainsail''' (böm′mān″sāl), ''n.'' A fore-and-aft mainsail, the foot of which is extended by a boom.

'''boomslang''' (böm′slang), ''n.'' [D. (in S. Africa), < ''boom'', tree, + ''slang'' (= OHG. ''slango'', MHG. ''slange'', G. ''schlange''), a snake, < *''slingen'', only in freq. ''slingeren'', turn, toss, sling, = OHG. ''slingan'', MHG. ''slingen'', G. ''schlingen'', wind, twist, sling, = E. ''sling'', q. v.] An African tree-snake, ''Bucephalus capensis''.

'''boomster''' (böm′stėr), ''n.'' [< ''boom''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ster''.] One engaged in booming the market or a political candidate for office; one who works up a boom. [Rare, U. S.]
{{smaller block|Moreover, he [the Secretary of the Interior] dismissed him “when under fire”—that is, while the Board’s enquiry was still in progress—an act which every ''boomster''}}

'''4.''' An unpaid service due by a tenant to his lord. [Now only prov. Eng.]

'''boon<sup>1</sup>''' (bön), ''v. t.'' [< ''boon''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 4.] To do gratuitous service to another, as a tenant to a landlord. ''Ray; Grose.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''boon<sup>2</sup>''' (bön), ''n.'' [Also E. dial. ''bun'' (see ''bun''<sup>2</sup>), < ME. ''bone'', later also ''bunne''; cf. Gael. and Ir. ''bunach'', coarse tow, the refuse of flax, < Gael. and Ir. ''bun'', stump, stock, root: see ''bun''<sup>2</sup>.] The refuse stalk of hemp or flax after the fiber has been removed by retting and breaking.

'''boon<sup>3</sup>''' (bön), ''a.'' [< ME. ''boon'', ''bone'', < Norm. F. ''boon'', OF. ''bon'', F. ''bon'', < L. ''bonus'', good: see ''bonus'', ''bonne'', ''bonny''<sup>1</sup>, etc.] '''1†.''' Good: as, ''boon'' cheer.—'''2†.''' Favorable; fortunate; prosperous: as, a ''boon'' voyage.—'''3†.''' Kind; bounteous; yielding abundance: as, “nature ''boon'',” ''Milton'', P. L., iv. 242.
{{smaller block|To a ''boon'' southern country he is fled.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Thyrsis.}}}}
'''4.''' Gay; merry; jolly; jovial; convivial: as, a ''boon'' companion; “jocund and ''boon'',” ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 793.
{{smaller block|Fled all the ''boon'' companions of the Earl.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}

'''boonage†''', ''n.'' [Also ''bonage''; < ''boon''<sup>1</sup>, 4, + ''-age''.] Boon-work.

'''boon-day†''' (bön′dā), ''n.'' A day on which boon-work was performed by a tenant for his lord, as in harvesting his crops.

'''boongary''' (böng′ga̤-ri), ''n.'' The native name of a tree-kangaroo, ''Dendrolagus lumholtzi'', of northern Queensland, Australia.

'''boonk''' (böngk), ''n.'' [Imitative, like ''bump''<sup>1</sup> and ''bumble'', ''n.'', q. v.] The little bittern of Europe, ''Ardetta minuta. Montagu.''

'''boon-loaf†''' (bön′lōf), ''n.'' A loaf allowed to a tenant when working on a boon-day.

'''boon-work''' (bön′wėrk), ''n.'' '''1.''' Unpaid work or service formerly rendered by a tenant to his lord; boon.—'''2.''' Work or service given gratuitously to a farmer by his neighbors on some special occasion.

'''boöpic''' (bō-op′ik), ''a.'' [< Gr. βοῶπις, ox-eyed: see ''boöps''.] Having eyes like those of an ox.

'''boöps''' (bō′ops), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. βοῶπις, ox-eyed, < βοῦς, ox (see ''Bos''), + ὤψ, eye.] An old book-name of the ''Box boöps'', a sparoid fish of the Mediterranean and the adjoining ocean. It is peculiar in the development of only one row of notched trenchant teeth in the jaws.

'''boor''' (bör), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''boore'', ''bour'' (also improp. ''bore'', ''boar''), possibly, in the form ''bour'' (mod. E. prop. *''bower'', bou′ėr) (cf. E. dial. ''bor'', neighbor, as a form of address), < ME. *''bour'', < AS. ''gebūr'', a dweller, husbandman, farmer, countryman (a word surviving without distinctive meaning in the compound ''neighbour'', ''neighbor'', < AS. ''neáh-gebūr''); but in the ordinary form and pronunciation, ''boor'', < LG. ''būr'', ''buur'', MLG. ''būr'', ''gebūr'', a husbandman, farmer, = D. ''buur'', MD. ''ghebure'', ''ghebuer'', neighbor, D. ''boer'', MD. ''geboer'' (a later form, prob. borrowed from LG.), a husbandman, farmer, rustic, knave

'''boorishly''' (bör′ish-li), ''adv.'' In a boorish manner.

'''boorishness''' (bör′ish-nes), ''n.'' [< ''boorish'' + ''-ness''.] The state of being boorish; clownishness; rusticity; coarseness of manners.

'''boos†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''boss''<sup>1</sup>. ''Chaucer.''

'''boose<sup>1</sup>''' (böz), ''n.'' [= Sc. ''boose'', ''buise'', ''buse''; < ME. ''boose'', ''bose'', < AS. *''bōs'' (represented only by the ONorth. ''bōsig'', > ''boosy''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.) = Icel. ''báss'' = Sw. ''bås'' = Dan. ''baas'', a cow-stall; cf. G. ''banse'', = Goth. ''bansts'', a barn.] A stall or inclosure for cattle. Also ''boosy'', ''bouse''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''boose<sup>2</sup>''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''booze''.

'''booser''', ''n.'' See ''boozer''.

'''boost<sup>1</sup>''' (böst), ''v. t.'' [Etym. unknown.] To lift or raise by pushing from behind, as a person climbing a tree; push up: often used figuratively: as, to ''boost'' a person over a fence, or into power. [North. U. S.]

'''boost<sup>1</sup>''' (böst), ''n.'' An upward shove or push; the act of boosting; the result of boosting; a lift, either literally or figuratively: as, to give one a ''boost''. [North. U. S.]

'''boost<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''boast''<sup>1</sup>.

'''boost<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.'' [Early mod. E., < ME. ''bost''; a variant of ''boist''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.] Same as ''boist''<sup>1</sup>.

'''boost<sup>4</sup>''' (böst), ''n.'' and ''v.'' Same as ''buist''.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|booming|627|boot}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''booming'''<sup>2</sup> (bö′ming), ''p. a.''   [Ppr. of ''boom''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.'']   Active; lively; advancing; buoyant: as, a ''booming'' market. [U. S.]

'''boom-iron''' (böm′ī″ėrn), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a metal ring on a yard, through which a studdingsail-boom is run in and out. {{img float|file=century v01 p0653 c1f1.png|width=215px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Boom-iron on yard-arm.}}}}

'''boom-jigger''' (böm′jig″ėr), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', the small purchase used in rigging out a studdingsail-boom, and, by shifting the tackle, in rigging it in. Also called ''in-and-out jigger''.

'''boomkin''' (böm′kin), ''n.'' Same as ''bumkin''.

'''boom-mainsail''' (böm′mān″sāl), ''n.'' A fore-and-aft mainsail, the foot of which is extended by a boom.

'''boomslang''' (böm′slang), ''n.''   [D. (in S. Africa), < ''boom'', tree, + ''slang'' (= OHG. ''slango'', MHG. ''slange'', G. ''schlange''), a snake, < *''slingen'', only in freq. ''slingeren'', turn, toss, sling, = OHG. ''slingan'', MHG. ''slingen'', G. ''schlingen'', wind, twist, sling, = E. ''sling'', q. v.]   An African tree-snake, ''Bucephalus capensis''.

'''boomster''' (böm′stėr), ''n.''   [< ''boom''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ster''.]   One engaged in booming the market or a political candidate for office; one who works up a boom. [Rare, U. S.]
{{smaller block|Moreover, he [the Secretary of the Interior] dismissed him “when under fire”—that is, while the Board’s enquiry was still in progress—an act which every ''boomster''}}

{{smaller block|must regard with loathing. {{right|''The Nation'', Feb. 12, 1880.}}}}

'''boom-tackle''' (böm′tak″l), ''n.'' A tackle consisting of a double and a single block and fall, used in guying out the main-boom of a fore-and-aft rigged vessel.

'''boon'''<sup>1</sup> (bön), ''n.''   [< ME. ''boon'', ''bone'', also ''boyn'', ''boyne'', < Icel. ''bōn'', a prayer, petition, with a parallel umlauted form ''bœn'' for *''bœn'' = Sw. Dan. ''bön'' = AS. ''bēn'', ME. ''ben'', ''bene'', a prayer: see ''ben''<sup>2</sup>. In the sense of ‘favor, privilege,’ there is confusion with ''boon''<sup>3</sup>.]   '''1†.''' A prayer; a petition.
{{smaller block|Our king unto God made his ''boon''. {{right|''Minot.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The wofull husbandman doth lowd complaine
To see his whole yeares labor lost so soone,
For which to God he made so many an idle ''boone''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vii. 34.}}}}
'''2.''' That which is asked; a favor; a thing desired; a benefaction.
{{smaller block|<poem>Vouchsafe me, for my meed, but one fair look;
A smaller ''boon'' than this I cannot beg.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., v. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|All our trade with the West Indies was a ''boon'', granted to us by the indulgence of England.
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Jan. 24, 1832.}}}}
Hence — '''3.''' A good; a benefit enjoyed; a blessing; a great privilege; a thing to be thankful for.
{{smaller block|The ''boon'' of religious freedom.
{{right|''Sydney Smith'', Peter Plymley’s Letters, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Is this the duty of rulers? Are men in such stations to give all that may be asked . . . without regarding whether it be a ''boon'' or a bane? {{right|''Brougham'', Lord North.}}}} '''4.''' An unpaid service due by a tenant to his lord. [Now only prov. Eng.]

'''boon<sup>1</sup>''' (bön), ''v. t.''   [< ''boon''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 4.]   To do gratuitous service to another, as a tenant to a landlord.   ''Ray; Grose.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''boon<sup>2</sup>''' (bön), ''n.''   [Also E. dial. ''bun'' (see ''bun''<sup>2</sup>), < ME. ''bone'', later also ''bunne''; cf. Gael. and Ir. ''bunach'', coarse tow, the refuse of flax, < Gael. and Ir. ''bun'', stump, stock, root: see ''bun''<sup>2</sup>.]   The refuse stalk of hemp or flax after the fiber has been removed by retting and breaking.

'''boon<sup>3</sup>''' (bön), ''a.''   [< ME. ''boon'', ''bone'', < Norm. F. ''boon'', OF. ''bon'', F. ''bon'', < L. ''bonus'', good: see ''bonus'', ''bonne'', ''bonny''<sup>1</sup>, etc.]   '''1†.''' Good: as, ''boon'' cheer.—'''2†.''' Favorable; fortunate; prosperous: as, a ''boon'' voyage.—'''3†.''' Kind; bounteous; yielding abundance: as, “nature ''boon'',” ''Milton'', P. L., iv. 242.
{{smaller block|To a ''boon'' southern country he is fled.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Thyrsis.}}}}
'''4.''' Gay; merry; jolly; jovial; convivial: as, a ''boon'' companion; “jocund and ''boon'',” ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 793.
{{smaller block|Fled all the ''boon'' companions of the Earl.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}

'''boonage†''', ''n.''   [Also ''bonage''; < ''boon''<sup>1</sup>, 4, + ''-age''.]   Boon-work.

'''boon-day†''' (bön′dā), ''n.'' A day on which boon-work was performed by a tenant for his lord, as in harvesting his crops.

'''boongary''' (böng′ga̤-ri), ''n.'' The native name of a tree-kangaroo, ''Dendrolagus lumholtzi'', of northern Queensland, Australia.

'''boonk''' (böngk), ''n.''   [Imitative, like ''bump''<sup>1</sup> and ''bumble'', ''n.'', q. v.]   The little bittern of Europe, ''Ardetta minuta. Montagu.''

'''boon-loaf†''' (bön′lōf), ''n.'' A loaf allowed to a tenant when working on a boon-day.

'''boon-work''' (bön′wėrk), ''n.'' '''1.''' Unpaid work or service formerly rendered by a tenant to his lord; boon.—'''2.''' Work or service given gratuitously to a farmer by his neighbors on some special occasion.

'''boöpic''' (bō-op′ik), ''a.''   [< Gr. βοῶπις, ox-eyed: see ''boöps''.]   Having eyes like those of an ox.

'''boöps''' (bō′ops), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. βοῶπις, ox-eyed, < βοῦς, ox (see ''Bos''), + ὤψ, eye.]   An old book-name of the ''Box boöps'', a sparoid fish of the Mediterranean and the adjoining ocean. It is peculiar in the development of only one row of notched trenchant teeth in the jaws.

'''boor''' (bör), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''boore'', ''bour'' (also improp. ''bore'', ''boar''), possibly, in the form ''bour'' (mod. E. prop. *''bower'', bou′ėr) (cf. E. dial. ''bor'', neighbor, as a form of address), < ME. *''bour'', < AS. ''gebūr'', a dweller, husbandman, farmer, countryman (a word surviving without distinctive meaning in the compound ''neighbour'', ''neighbor'', < AS. ''neáh-gebūr''); but in the ordinary form and pronunciation, ''boor'', < LG. ''būr'', ''buur'', MLG. ''būr'', ''gebūr'', a husbandman, farmer, = D. ''buur'', MD. ''ghebure'', ''ghebuer'', neighbor, D. ''boer'', MD. ''geboer'' (a later form, prob. borrowed from LG.), a husbandman, farmer, rustic, knave at cards, = OHG. ''gibūr'', ''gibūro'', MHG. ''gebūr'', ''gebūre'', G. ''bauer'', a husbandman, peasant, rustic, = AS. ''gebūr'', as above; lit. one who occupies the same dwelling (house, village, farm) with another, one who dwells with or near another (a sense more definitely expressed by the AS. ''neáh-gebūr'', ‘nigh-dweller,’ neighbor: see ''neighbor''), < ''ge-'', together, a generalizing or coördinating prefix (see ''ge-''), + ''būr'', > E. ''bower'', a dwelling: see ''bower''<sup>1</sup>. The forms, as those of others from the same root (AS. ''būan'', dwell, etc.), are somewhat confused in the several languages. See ''bower''<sup>1</sup>, ''bower''<sup>5</sup>, ''bower''<sup>6</sup>, etc., and ''neighbor''.]   '''1.''' A countryman; a peasant; a rustic; a clown; particularly, a Dutch or German peasant.
{{smaller block|Knave meant once no more than lad; . . . villain than peasant; a ''boor'' was only a farmer; a varlet was but a serving-man; . . . a churl but a strong fellow.
{{right|''Abp. Trench'', Study of Words, p. 56.}}}}
{{smaller block|There were others, the ''boors'', who seem to have had no land of their own, but worked on the lord’s private land like the laborers of to-day.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 316.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' One who is rude in manners, or illiterate; a clown; a clownish person.
{{smaller block|The profoundest philosopher differs in degree only, not in kind, from the most uncultivated ''boor''.
{{right|''Channing'', Perfect Life, p. 172.}}}}
{{smaller block|The habits and cunning of a ''boor''. {{right|''Thackeray''.}}}}
{{smaller block|Tramped down by that Northern ''boor'', Peter the Great.
{{right|''D. G. Mitchell'', Wet Days.}}}}
'''3.''' [''cap.''] Same as ''Boer''.

'''boord<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' An obsolete form of ''board''.

'''boord<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' A variant form of ''bourd''<sup>1</sup>.

'''boorish''' (bör′ish), ''a.''   [< ''boor'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>; = D. ''boersch'' = G. ''bäuerisch'', clownish, rustic.]   '''1.''' Resembling a boor; clownish; rustic; awkward in manners; illiterate.
{{smaller block|<poem>No lusty neatherd thither drove his kine,
No ''boorish'' hogherd fed his rooting swine.</poem>
{{right|''W. Browne'', Brit. Past., ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Pertaining to or fit for a boor.
{{smaller block|A gross and ''boorish'' opinion.
{{right|''Milton'', On Divorce, i. 9.}}}}

{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' ''Boorish, Churlish, Clownish, Loutish.'' He who is ''boorish'' is so low-bred in habits and ways as to be positively offensive. He who is ''churlish'' offends by his language and manners, they being such as would naturally be found in one who is coarse and selfish, and therefore generally insolent or crusty and rough; the opposite of ''kind'' and ''courteous'': as, it is ''churlish'' to refuse to answer a civil question. The opposite of ''boorish'' is ''refined'' or ''polite''; the opposite of ''clownish'' is ''elegant''. ''Clownish'' is a somewhat weaker word than ''boorish'', implying less that is disgusting in manner and speech; it often notes mere lack of refinement. The difference between ''clownish'' and ''loutish'' is that he who is ''clownish'' is generally stupid and sometimes ludicrous, while he who is ''loutish'' is perhaps slovenly and worthy of blame.}}

{{smaller block|In some countries the large cities absorb the wealth and fashion of the nation, . . . and the country is inhabited almost entirely by ''boorish'' peasantry.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 80.}}}}
<poem>My master is of ''churlish'' disposition,
And little recks to find the way to heaven
By doing deeds of hospitality.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|’Tis ''clownish'' to insist on doing all with one’s own hands, as if every man should build his own clumsy house, forge his hammer, and bake his dough.
{{right|''Emerson'', Success.}}}}

{{smaller block|He [Lord Chesterfield] labored for years to mould his dull, heavy, ''loutish'' son, Stanhope, into a graceful man of fashion. {{right|''W. Mathews'', Getting on in the World, p. 42.}}}}

'''boorishly''' (bör′ish-li), ''adv.'' In a boorish manner.
{{smaller block|Limbs . . . neither weak nor ''boorishly'' robust. {{right|''Fenton'', tr. of Martial’s Epigrams, x. 47.}}}}

'''boorishness''' (bör′ish-nes), ''n.''   [< ''boorish'' + ''-ness''.]   The state of being boorish; clownishness; rusticity; coarseness of manners.

'''boornouse''' (bör-nös′), ''n.'' Same as ''burnoose''.

'''boos†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''boss''<sup>1</sup>.   ''Chaucer.''

'''boose<sup>1</sup>''' (böz), ''n.''   [= Sc. ''boose'', ''buise'', ''buse''; < ME. ''boose'', ''bose'', < AS. *''bōs'' (represented only by the ONorth. ''bōsig'', > ''boosy''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.) = Icel. ''báss'' = Sw. ''bås'' = Dan. ''baas'', a cow-stall; cf. G. ''banse'', = Goth. ''bansts'', a barn.]   A stall or inclosure for cattle. Also ''boosy'', ''bouse''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''boose<sup>2</sup>''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''booze''.

'''booser''', ''n.'' See ''boozer''.

'''boost<sup>1</sup>''' (böst), ''v. t.''   [Etym. unknown.]   To lift or raise by pushing from behind, as a person climbing a tree; push up: often used figuratively: as, to ''boost'' a person over a fence, or into power. [North. U. S.]

'''boost<sup>1</sup>''' (böst), ''n.'' An upward shove or push; the act of boosting; the result of boosting; a lift, either literally or figuratively: as, to give one a ''boost''. [North. U. S.]

'''boost<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''boast''<sup>1</sup>.

'''boost<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.''   [Early mod. E., < ME. ''bost''; a variant of ''boist''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   Same as ''boist''<sup>1</sup>.

'''boost<sup>4</sup>''' (böst), ''n.'' and ''v.'' Same as ''buist''.

'''boosy<sup>1</sup>''' (bö′zi), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''boosey'', ''bousie'', < ME. (not found), < AS. (ONorth.) ''bōsig'', ''bōsih'', < *''bōs'', a stall: see ''boose''<sup>1</sup>.]   Same as ''boose''<sup>1</sup>.

'''boosy<sup>2</sup>''', ''a.'' See ''boozy''.

'''boot<sup>1</sup>''' (böt), ''n.''   [< ME. ''boote'', ''bote'', ''bot'', < AS. ''bōt'', advantage, amendment, reparation (esp. in the phrase ''tō bōte'' (lit. ‘for reparation,’ E. ''to boot''), frequent in the AS. laws), = OS. ''bōta'' = OFries. ''bōte'' = D. ''boete'' = LG. ''bote'' = OHG. ''buoza'', MHG. ''buoze'', G. ''busse'' = Icel. ''bōt'' = Sw. ''bot'' = Dan. ''bod'' = Goth. ''bōta'', boot, advantage, profit, repair, reparation, etc.; < Teut. *''batan'' (pret. *''bōt''), be good, be useful, profit, avail, whence ult. E. ''bet''<sup>1</sup>, ''better''<sup>1</sup>, ''batten''<sup>1</sup>, ''battle''<sup>3</sup>, etc., and (as a deriv. of ''boot''), ''beet''<sup>2</sup>, mend, repair: see these words.]   '''1†.''' Profit; gain; advantage.
{{smaller block|If then the reward bee to bee measured by thy merites, what ''boote'' canst thou seeke for, but eternall paine.
{{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 181.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O! spare thy happy daies, and them apply
To better ''boot''. ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. xi. 19.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Something which is thrown in by one of the parties to a bargain as an additional consideration, or to make the exchange equal.
{{smaller block|I’ll give you ''boot'', I’ll give you three for one.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iv. 5.}}}}
'''3†.''' Help or deliverance; assistance; relief; remedy: as, ''boot'' for every bale.
{{smaller block|She is . . . the rote of bountee . . . and soules ''bote''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prioress’s Tale, l. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|Anon he yaf the syke man his ''bote''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 424.}}}}
{{smaller block|Next her son, our soul’s best ''boot''. {{right|''Wordsworth.''}}}}

'''4†.''' Resource; alternative.

{{smaller block|There was none other ''boote'' for him, but to arm him.
{{right|''Lord Berners'', tr. of Froissart, I. 674.}}}}

'''It is no boot,''' it is useless or of no avail.

{{smaller block|Whereupon we thought it ''no boot'' to sit longer, since we could escape unobserved.
{{right|''R. Knox'', Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 418.}}}}

'''To boot'''   [AS. ''tō bōte''], to the advantage; into the bargain; in addition; over and above; besides: as, I will give my house for yours with $500 ''to boot.''

<poem>Helen to change would give an eye ''to boot.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|We are a people of prayer and good works ''to boot.''
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Old Manse, I.}}}}

'''To make boot of,''' to make profit of; gain by.

<poem>Give him no breath, but now
''Make boot of'' his distraction.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 1.}}}}

'''boot<sup>1</sup>''' (böt), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bōten'', profit, < ''bote'', boot, profit. The earlier verb was AS. ''bētan'', > ME. ''beten'', mod. E. ''beet'': see ''beet''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' To profit; advantage; avail: now only used impersonally: as, it ''boots'' us little.

<poem>What ''bootes'' it al to have, and nothing use?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. vi. 17.}}}}
<poem>For what I have, I need not to repeat;
And what I want, it ''boots'' not to complain.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 4.}}}}

'''2†.''' To present into the bargain; enrich; benefit.

<poem>I will ''boot'' thee with what gift beside
Thy modesty can beg.     ''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 5.</poem><noinclude><references/></noinclude>
